title: Simone de Beauvoir: The Second Sex and the Ethics of Ambiguity
subtitle: Why no one is simply born a woman, and why no one is free alone
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what Beauvoir meant by “one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman”.
By the end you will be able to describe how women have been made the Other, and the roles of myth, situation and complicity in that process.
By the end you will be able to explain Beauvoir's idea of ambiguity and why, for her, my freedom requires the freedom of others.
By the end you will be able to compare Beauvoir's existentialism with Sartre's.
By the end you will be able to assess the main criticisms of *The Second Sex* and its influence on later feminism.
hook:
In the late 1940s Simone de Beauvoir set out to write about herself. She later recalled that when she asked what being a woman had meant for her, she was at first tempted to answer that it had meant nothing much. Sartre suggested she look more closely: she had not been brought up the way a boy would have been. She looked, and what she found changed her project and the twentieth century. She discovered that the world she had grown up in was organised around men as the norm and women as the exception, the second sex.

The result, *The Second Sex* (1949), was a two-volume, roughly thousand-page study drawing on biology, psychoanalysis, Marxism, history, myth, literature and the details of everyday life. It provoked outrage in France, was placed on the Catholic Church's Index of Forbidden Books, and became one of the founding texts of modern feminism. Its most famous sentence is only a few words long: one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. Today you meet the philosopher behind it, who was far more than Sartre's companion.

sections.heading: A Dutiful Daughter Who Refused
sections.body:
Simone de Beauvoir (1908–1986) was born in Paris into a respectable Catholic family whose fortunes were in decline. Her mother was devout; her father was a sceptical lawyer who loved literature and the theatre. Because the family could not provide a large dowry, her father reportedly said that Simone would have to work for a living, and he half-admiringly said she had a man's brain. As a teenager she lost her religious faith and resolved to become a writer. Her memoir, *Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter* (1958), describes this escape from a confined bourgeois girlhood.

She studied philosophy at the Sorbonne and in 1929, at twenty-one, came second in the *agrégation*, the national examination for philosophy teachers, among the youngest ever to pass it. First place went to Jean-Paul Sartre (Day 77), who was retaking it. Some examiners reportedly debated which of the two deserved first place. The two began a partnership that lasted until Sartre's death in 1980: they never married, never lived together, read every draft of each other's work and kept an open relationship that included other lovers.

That relationship has a darker side that honest accounts must mention. Several of Beauvoir's affairs were with her own former female students, some of whom she later introduced to Sartre. In 1943 she was suspended from her teaching post after a complaint from a student's mother. Letters published after her death have led many readers to judge her conduct harshly.

Beauvoir taught in lycées until 1943, then lived by her writing: novels such as *She Came to Stay* (1943) and *The Mandarins* (1954), which won the Prix Goncourt, France's most famous literary prize; philosophical essays; and a multi-volume autobiography. She often called herself a writer rather than a philosopher, and for decades she was treated as Sartre's disciple. Many scholars now argue this badly underrates her originality.

sections.heading: The Ethics of Ambiguity
sections.body:
Before *The Second Sex*, Beauvoir tried to do something Sartre promised but never completed: write an existentialist ethics. *The Ethics of Ambiguity* (1947) begins from the human condition as she saw it. We are **ambiguous** beings. We are free consciousnesses, able to choose and transcend any situation, yet we are also bodies, objects in the world, mortal, dependent and shaped by others. We are, at once, subjects and things.

Most philosophies, she argued, try to escape this ambiguity by denying one side: either treating us as pure minds or as mere matter. An honest ethics must accept both. Since there is no God and no human nature (as Sartre had argued), values do not exist ready-made. They come into the world through human freedom. But this does not mean anything goes.

Beauvoir's key move is this. If I truly value freedom, the source of all value, I cannot value only my own. My projects need a world of other free people, to receive them, continue them, argue with them and give them meaning. A painting no one can see, a book no one can read, a cause no one else can join, is empty. So, she wrote, to will oneself free is also to will others free. Oppression is wrong because it cuts people off from their future, reducing them to mere objects, and freedom is only fulfilled when it reaches for the freedom of others.

She also offers a vivid gallery of ways people flee freedom, a little like Sartre's bad faith but more social:

- **The sub-man** avoids passion and commitment, shrinking his life to nothing.
- **The serious man** submerges his freedom in some cause, idol or institution (the Party, the Nation, Wealth) and treats it as an absolute that justifies anything, even sacrificing others.
- **The adventurer** throws himself into exploits for their own sake, indifferent to their effects on others.
- **The passionate man** devotes himself so completely to one object or person that the rest of the world disappears.

Genuine freedom, by contrast, commits itself to projects while remembering that they matter only because free people give them meaning.

She notices too that some people, like children, live in a ready-made world of given values not by fault but by situation. Some adults are kept in a childlike condition by others: slaves and, in many societies, women. That observation would become the seed of her most famous book.

sections.heading: She Is the Other
sections.body:
*The Second Sex* opens with a question: what is a woman? Beauvoir rejects two easy answers. It is not enough to point to biology, since not every female human counts as a “real woman” by society's standards; people constantly worry that women are losing their femininity, as if it were something one could lose. Nor can we simply deny that women exist as a group; that would be a flight from reality.

Her answer begins with a striking asymmetry. A man never needs to begin by declaring that he is a man; he is simply a human being. Man is treated as the neutral, the standard, the positive; woman as the deviation, defined in relation to him. In her own memorable formulation, he is the Subject, the Absolute, and she is the **Other**.

The idea of the Other comes partly from Hegel's master and slave (Day 59) and partly from Sartre's look (Day 77). Every consciousness, Beauvoir argued, tends to define itself by setting itself against something else: natives against foreigners, one group against another. Usually this is reciprocal: I am a foreigner to them as they are to me. What is unique about the relation between the sexes is that it has hardened into a one-way relationship. Men have set themselves up as the essential subject, and women have been fixed as the inessential other.

Why have women accepted this? Beauvoir's answers are historical rather than biological: women lacked their own past, religion and solidarity as a group, since they were scattered among men, attached to fathers and husbands by class and family more than to other women. And she adds an uncomfortable point. Being the Other has certain comforts. A woman who accepts a protected, dependent role is spared the anguish and risk of freedom. This **complicity**, a version of bad faith, is part of what keeps the system going, though it is far from the whole story, since women have usually had few real alternatives.

sections.heading: One Is Not Born, but Becomes, a Woman
sections.body:
The second volume of *The Second Sex* opens with its most famous sentence: one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. This is existence precedes essence applied to sex. There is no eternal feminine essence, no fixed female nature, that makes women passive, emotional or domestic. What we call femininity is produced over a lifetime by upbringing, expectations, laws and economic conditions.

Beauvoir follows this process in painstaking detail, from childhood to old age. A little boy is encouraged to climb trees, fight and explore; his body is a tool for acting on the world. A little girl is given a doll, a passive double of herself, and praised for being pretty and good. She learns to see herself as an object to be looked at. At adolescence she discovers that the world expects her to wait, to please, to be chosen. Marriage, housework and motherhood, as organised in her society, often confine her to **immanence**: repetitive tasks that maintain life but never build anything new. Men, meanwhile, are free for **transcendence**: projects, work, politics and creation that push into the future.

Biology is real, Beauvoir insists. Women's bodies do differ, and pregnancy and menstruation shape women's experience. But biology is not destiny. The body is always lived within a **situation**, a set of social meanings and material conditions. The fact that women bear children does not by itself dictate that they must be excluded from public life; societies decide what that fact means.

The book also dissects the **myths** of woman in literature and religion: woman as mother, as virgin, as temptress, as nature, as mystery. These myths contradict one another, which shows that they say more about men's hopes and fears than about real women.

Beauvoir ends not with despair but with a call. Women's liberation requires economic independence, which she regarded as the first condition, and also social change, so that women and men can recognise each other as equals, each both subject and object. She hoped men and women would one day affirm their **brotherhood**, as she put it, beyond their natural differences.

sections.heading: Reception, Influence and Criticism
sections.body:
The reaction in 1949 was ferocious. The Catholic novelist François Mauriac attacked the book publicly, and Beauvoir received obscene letters. Yet it sold strongly from the start. An English translation appeared in 1953, but it was heavily abridged and mistranslated philosophical terms; a complete new translation by Constance Borde and Sheila Malovany-Chevallier appeared in 2009.

When the second wave of feminism arose in the 1960s and 1970s, many activists found their starting point in Beauvoir. Betty Friedan's *The Feminine Mystique* (1963), Kate Millett and Shulamith Firestone all owe her something. Beauvoir herself became an active feminist in the 1970s, signing the 1971 Manifesto of the 343, in which women declared they had had abortions, then illegal in France. She also wrote a major study of how societies treat the elderly, *Old Age* (1970), applying the same method to another group made Other.

Later thinkers pressed hard criticisms:

- **Whose women?** Beauvoir wrote mostly from the experience of white, middle-class European women. Black feminists such as bell hooks and theorists of intersectionality argued that race, class and colonialism shape womanhood in ways she treated only briefly, even as she drew analogies to racism and colonialism.
- **Masculine ideals?** Some feminists argued that she valued transcendence, public action and independence, traditionally male ideals, while looking down on motherhood, care and the body. Carol Gilligan and care ethicists (Day 85) would revalue these.
- **Sex and gender.** Later theorists distinguished biological sex from social gender, and Judith Butler, in *Gender Trouble* (1990), pushed Beauvoir's idea further, arguing that gender is performed through repeated acts. Whether Beauvoir herself drew such a clear line between sex and gender is debated.
- **Too pessimistic about women's agency?** Some historians argue she underestimated how women had always resisted and created culture.

Even critics generally agree that she made one move that changed everything: she showed that what seemed natural was historical, and therefore could be changed.

sections.heading: Beauvoir and Sartre: Who Thought What?
sections.body:
Beauvoir and Sartre shared a framework, but their differences matter, and many scholars now think several of them favour Beauvoir.

First, **situation**. Early Sartre, in *Being and Nothingness* (Day 77), suggested that freedom is absolute: even a prisoner is free to choose the meaning of his chains. Beauvoir, from the start, insisted that situations can genuinely limit freedom. A woman confined to a harem, she argued, cannot simply choose her way out; oppression is real precisely because it closes off possibilities. Sartre later moved toward her view.

Second, **others**. Sartre's early account of relations between people is a struggle in which each tries to objectify the other (remember *No Exit*). Beauvoir's ethics makes others the condition of my freedom, not merely its threat. Reciprocity, friendship and recognition are real possibilities, not just illusions.

Third, **the body**. Beauvoir's careful attention to embodied, lived experience, including the experience of menstruation, sexuality, pregnancy and ageing, owes much to her friend Maurice Merleau-Ponty and the phenomenology you met with Husserl (Day 75). It goes beyond anything Sartre wrote.

The partnership also tells us something about how philosophy has been written. For decades textbooks listed Beauvoir as an existentialist novelist and Sartre as the philosopher. Recovering women's contributions, from Hypatia to Wollstonecraft (Day 54) to Beauvoir, is part of what she herself would call refusing to let women remain the Other in history.

keyQuote.text: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
keyQuote.source: Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex (1949), opening of Volume II

modernConnection.title: The Default Human: Designing for the Subject and Forgetting the Other
modernConnection.body:
Beauvoir's claim that man is treated as the neutral human and woman as the deviation can sound abstract. Modern data make it concrete. In *Invisible Women* (2019), the journalist Caroline Criado Perez collected examples of a world designed around a male default. For decades the standard crash-test dummies used in car safety testing were modelled on an average male body, and studies have found women more likely to be seriously injured in comparable crashes. Office temperature standards were long based on the metabolic rate of a typical man. Medical research historically under-enrolled women, so some drug doses and descriptions of heart-attack symptoms fitted men better. Voice recognition systems and smartphones have been reported to work less well for women's voices and hands.

None of this required anyone to hate women. That is exactly Beauvoir's point. When one group is unconsciously treated as the standard human, the other becomes an afterthought, the Other, measured against a norm that was never neutral.

Her idea that we become women also echoes in debates about toys, school subjects and careers. Researchers study how girls and boys are steered from early childhood: pink and blue aisles, assumptions about who is good at maths, who gets interrupted in meetings. The point is not that every difference between the sexes is invented, but that social expectations magnify and shape whatever differences exist.

Be honest about the limits. Many of these gaps have narrowed since 1949, and in some areas, such as university enrolment in many countries, women now outnumber men. Some researchers argue that certain sex differences in interests have biological roots, a debate Beauvoir's framework must take seriously rather than dismiss. And today's debates about gender identity raise questions Beauvoir never addressed, with people on several sides claiming her legacy. Still, her central tool remains powerful: whenever something presents itself as neutral and natural, ask who it was designed for, and who was made the Other.

vocabulary.definition: In Beauvoir, the position of a group defined only in relation to a dominant group that sees itself as the norm or essential subject; she argued women have been made the Other to men.
vocabulary.example: Calling a sport “football” for men but “women's football” for women treats women as the Other.

vocabulary.definition: Beauvoir's term for the human condition of being both free subjects and embodied, dependent objects, a tension an honest ethics must accept rather than escape.
vocabulary.example: A surgeon is a free agent shaping a patient's future, and also a tired body that needs sleep: both sides of human ambiguity.

vocabulary.definition: The concrete social, bodily and material circumstances within which freedom operates, which can genuinely enlarge or restrict what choices are possible.
vocabulary.example: Beauvoir argued that a woman's situation in 1940s France, without economic independence, limited her freedom in ways no attitude could overcome.

vocabulary.definition: For Beauvoir, a condition of repetition and maintenance that keeps life going but creates nothing new and opens no future.
vocabulary.example: Washing the same dishes every day, with no project beyond it, is Beauvoir's image of immanence.

vocabulary.definition: Free activity that projects itself into the future through creative work, action and new projects.
vocabulary.example: Writing a book, founding a company or campaigning for a law are forms of transcendence.

vocabulary.definition: Beauvoir's term for the ways members of an oppressed group may accept their subordinate role because it spares them the risks and anguish of freedom.
vocabulary.example: Beauvoir noted the temptation of complicity for a woman who accepts dependence in exchange for protection.

vocabulary.definition: In *The Ethics of Ambiguity*, someone who hands over his freedom to an external cause or idol, treating it as an absolute that justifies anything.
vocabulary.example: An official who says the Party is always right, even when it commits atrocities, is Beauvoir's serious man.

vocabulary.definition: The feminist movement of the 1960s–1980s, which went beyond the vote to address work, family, sexuality, reproduction and culture; Beauvoir was one of its key inspirations.
vocabulary.example: Campaigns for legal abortion and equal pay in the 1970s were central to second-wave feminism.

thinkingExercise.title: How Did You Become You?
thinkingExercise.prompt: Apply Beauvoir's method of tracing how a social identity is formed over a lifetime, whether gender or another identity that matters to you.
steps: Choose an identity you have: your gender, or another such as your nationality, class or profession.
List three messages you received in childhood or adolescence about how someone like you should behave. Who sent them: family, school, media, peers?
For each message, ask: which parts reflect a real fact about bodies or circumstances, and which parts are social expectation presented as nature?
Identify one way in which you have been treated as the norm, and one way in which you have been treated as the Other. How did each feel?
Write a paragraph applying Beauvoir's principle that to will oneself free is also to will others free: what would it mean in one relationship in your life?

summary: Simone de Beauvoir (1908–1986) was a philosopher, novelist and memoirist, long treated as Sartre's follower but now widely recognised as an original thinker.
*The Ethics of Ambiguity* (1947) argues that humans are ambiguous, both free subjects and embodied objects, and that to will oneself free is also to will others free.
*The Second Sex* (1949) argues that man has been treated as the Subject and woman as the Other, a one-sided relationship sustained by history, myth and sometimes complicity.
“One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman”: femininity is not a fixed essence but is produced through upbringing and situation; biology matters, but it is not destiny.
Beauvoir stressed situation, embodiment and reciprocity more than early Sartre, and her work inspired second-wave feminism.
Critics have challenged her focus on white middle-class women, her preference for transcendence over care, and her views on sex and gender.

quiz.question: What does Beauvoir mean by “one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman”?
options: Biological sex is a complete illusion
Girls choose to become women at a certain age
Femininity is shaped by upbringing, expectations and situation rather than being a fixed natural essence
Only women who have children are real women
quiz.explanation: It applies existence precedes essence to sex: what counts as being a woman is produced socially over a lifetime, though Beauvoir did not deny biological facts.

quiz.question: In Beauvoir's analysis, what is distinctive about women as the Other?
options: The relation is not reciprocal: men set themselves up as the essential subject and fix women as inessential
Women have always defined men as the Other too, equally
Women are a numerical minority
Women chose this role freely in a historical contract
quiz.explanation: Most self–other relations are reciprocal, but between the sexes the relationship hardened into a one-way hierarchy.

quiz.question: Beauvoir argued that because biology is unimportant, the female body plays no role in women's experience.
quiz.explanation: She took biology and the body seriously, but argued that the body is always lived within a situation; biology is not destiny.

quiz.question: Why, according to *The Ethics of Ambiguity*, must I will the freedom of others?
options: Because God commands it
Because the law requires it
Because others will punish me otherwise
Because my own projects need a world of free people to give them meaning
quiz.explanation: Freedom is the source of value, and my projects only matter if other free people can take them up; so to will oneself free is also to will others free.

quiz.question: A party official says the cause is so important that any sacrifice of individuals is justified. Which of Beauvoir's types fits best?
options: The adventurer
The serious man
The sub-man
The independent woman
quiz.explanation: The serious man hands his freedom over to an absolute cause and treats it as justifying anything, including oppression.

quiz.question: Which pair best captures Beauvoir's contrast between traditional women's and men's roles?
options: Reason and emotion
Being and nothingness
Ready-to-hand and present-at-hand
Immanence and transcendence
quiz.explanation: She argued women were confined to immanence, repetitive maintenance, while men were free for transcendence, creative projects.

quiz.question: Beauvoir held, earlier and more firmly than the young Sartre, that a person's situation can genuinely restrict freedom.
quiz.explanation: Early Sartre made freedom nearly absolute; Beauvoir insisted that oppression really closes off possibilities, and Sartre later moved toward her view.

quiz.question: Car crash-test dummies modelled for decades on an average male body best illustrate which of Beauvoir's ideas?
options: Man treated as the neutral human standard and woman as the Other
Immanence
The ethics of the adventurer
The myth of the eternal mother
quiz.explanation: Treating the male body as the default human body is a concrete case of man as the Subject and woman as the deviation.

quiz.question: The first English translation of *The Second Sex* (1953) was complete and is still considered the most accurate.
quiz.explanation: It was heavily abridged and mistranslated philosophical terms; a complete new translation appeared in 2009.

quiz.question: Which is a criticism later feminists made of *The Second Sex*?
options: It ignored biology entirely
It was too favourable to the Catholic Church
It generalised from the experience of white, middle-class European women
It argued that women are naturally inferior
quiz.explanation: Black feminists and intersectional theorists argued that race, class and colonialism shape womanhood in ways Beauvoir treated only briefly.

goDeeper.body:
Three scholarly debates make Beauvoir richer on a second reading. The first is the **sex/gender question**. English-speaking feminists in the 1970s often read *The Second Sex* as the origin of the distinction between biological sex and social gender. Yet Beauvoir never used that pair of terms, and some scholars, such as Toril Moi, argue that her concept of the lived body dissolves the distinction instead: the body is never mere biology, but always a body in a situation. Judith Butler's *Gender Trouble* went in another direction, suggesting that even sex is shaped by social practices. Reading Beauvoir alongside both sides is a good exercise in seeing how a classic is reinterpreted.

The second debate is about **her originality**. Kate and Edward Fullbrook argued, provocatively, that key ideas of *Being and Nothingness* first appear in Beauvoir's novel *She Came to Stay*. Margaret Simons, editor of many of her philosophical writings, showed that Beauvoir's student diaries from 1927, before she met Sartre, already worked on the problem of self and other. Others think the influence ran both ways in a genuine dialogue.

The third concerns **old age**. In *Old Age* (1970) Beauvoir argued that the elderly, too, are made Other, treated as a burden or a stereotype rather than as free subjects with projects. Her method, tracing how a social category is constructed through institutions, economics and myth, has since been applied to disability, race and age, showing that *The Second Sex* offered not only conclusions about women but a general way of seeing.

readings.title: The Second Sex
readings.author: Simone de Beauvoir
readings.note: Read the Introduction and the opening chapter of Volume II, “Childhood”. The 2009 Borde and Malovany-Chevallier translation is complete.

readings.title: The Ethics of Ambiguity
readings.author: Simone de Beauvoir
readings.note: Short and readable; Part II contains the portraits of the sub-man, the serious man and the adventurer.

readings.title: Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter
readings.author: Simone de Beauvoir
readings.note: Her vivid account of growing up and escaping a confined bourgeois girlhood.

readings.author: Kate Kirkpatrick
readings.note: A recent biography that uses newly available diaries and letters to present her as an original philosopher.

questions: Which differences between the sexes, if any, do you think are natural, and which are made? How could we find out?
Is Beauvoir right that freedom requires the freedom of others, or can one person be free in an unfree society?
Should Beauvoir's personal conduct affect how we read her philosophy? Compare your answer with the case of Heidegger (Day 76).
